{"id": "59:9/q05", "question": "How are 'the abode and faith' grammatically and rhetorically joined?", "turns_on": "Faith is not literally a place; analyses supply a verb or place, use metaphor, or read the conjunction as accompaniment.", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q05/p1", "position": "An omitted fitting verb governs faith: they settled the city and embraced, chose, or made sincere their faith.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī and the majority cite Arabic coordination of unlike objects, including 'fed her straw and [gave] cold water'; Samarrāʾī cites drinking milk and eating dates, and 10:71 requires assembling partners beside gathering a plan. Al-Ṭabarṣī says coordination is in wording, not sense. Al-Baghawī says faith is not a place; Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports an omitted verb meaning they preferred faith. Qurṭubī also reports omitted words referring to faith's places."}, {"id": "59:9/q05/p2", "position": "Faith is a figurative dwelling in which the Anṣār were firmly established.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī say steadfast faith is like a home; Abū ʿAlī cites settling among a clan's elite. Ālūsī prefers the implicit metaphor, while al-Samīn notes the debated combination of literal and figurative senses. Biqāʿī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī emphasize abiding and making religious practice possible. Qurṭubī reports metaphorically settling faith."}, {"id": "59:9/q05/p3", "position": "The wording implicitly means 'abode of migration and abode of faith,' or calls Medina 'faith'.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī offers ellipsis of abode or calling Medina faith as the place it appeared; al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī and others report these. Bursevī favors 'abode of faith'; al-Samīn challenges whether the article can replace a possessive complement, noting Kufan and Basran disagreement and 79:39. Ālūsī rejects both parses as strained."}, {"id": "59:9/q05/p4", "position": "Faith accompanies the abode as a comitative object: they settled there with faith.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the pairing eloquent; Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers the comitative waw and argues its noun need not share the verb's government, against the Basran restriction and Ibn Hishām's doubt that it occurs certainly in the Qur'an; Kufans, Akhfash, and ʿAbd al-Qāhir allow the waw itself to govern. Elmalılı likes avoiding ellipsis; Ālūsī rejects the parse."}, {"id": "59:9/q05/p5", "position": "The verb takes an expanded sense of adhering to the abode and faith together.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and Abū Ḥayyān allow tabawwaʾū to imply adherence; Bursevī reports this alongside treating spiritual state as place; al-Irshād sees observance of faith's public rights. Ālūsī notes metonymy of settling for staying. Qurṭubī reports taking the verb as adhering to abode and faith."}, {"id": "59:9/q05/p6", "position": "The Anṣār prepared the abode through faith.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu prefers the sense 'prepare' because the Anṣār already owned their land; the Aqaba pledge secured it as an Islamic abode. Elmalılı permits this lexical sense."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q06", "question": "What does 'before them' refer to and what came first?", "turns_on": "Whether it dates their settlement before migrants arrived, their belief before some migrants, or precedence in settled faith.", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q06/p1", "position": "Before the emigrants arrived or migrated to Medina; the Anṣār had established abode and faith there.", "reasons": "Mujāhid identifies the pronoun; Maqātil distinguishes prior settlement from faith. The verse does not require Anṣār belief before all emigrants, say Qurṭubī, Bursevī, and Ālūsī. Biqāʿī restricts the comparison to migration, not the whole mission; Ibn ʿĀshūr attaches the phrase only to settlement on his comitative parse. Al-Zajjāj assigns the pronoun to emigrants."}, {"id": "59:9/q06/p2", "position": "They believed before many emigrants, or before the emigrants in view.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr limits priority to many, not all; Ṭabarṣī reports a view of the seventy at Aqaba believing before the emigrants and pledging to fight all peoples."}, {"id": "59:9/q06/p3", "position": "Inwardly, before migration from the exile of the lower soul to the primordial home.", "reasons": "Qāshānī cites 'love of homeland is part of faith' and contrasts residents who kept purity with wayfarers who regained it."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q07", "question": "Whom do they love and how is that love shown?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q07/p1", "position": "They love emigrant believers who came to Medina, welcoming and supporting them.", "reasons": "Maqātil, Ṭabarī and others identify the migrants; Ālūsī offers literal love for faith-driven migration or a figure for unworn support. Biqāʿī says choosing the Anṣār as destination deepens the claim; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites brotherhood, Saʿd ibn al-Rabīʿ's offer, and unusual tribal welcome. Reports recount date-palm sharing, Bahrain land refused without migrant parity, and migrants praising the Anṣār. Elmalılı includes the Prophet and rich or poor migrants. Al-Dāmghānī says ḥubb can mean preferring, citing 38:32, 14:3, 9:23, 16:107 and 41:17; al-Naḥḥās glosses hājara ilayhim as moving to them."}, {"id": "59:9/q07/p2", "position": "Inwardly, it is affinity and true kinship among those sharing primordial purity.", "reasons": "Qāshānī invokes the first covenant and brotherhood of fellow wayfarers; Bursevī says lovers of God love whom God and His beloved love."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q08", "question": "What is the 'need' they do not find in their breasts?", "turns_on": "Whether ḥājah is desire for the goods, resentment about them, or a felt lack.", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q08/p1", "position": "No envy, anger, resentment, or distress over the migrants' preference and gifts.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan glosses it as envy; al-Rāzī explains 'need' as metonym for these accompanying emotions. Al-Wāḥidī says a ḥājah is anything burdensome in the breast needing removal. Bayḍāwī includes requests; several authors point to the Anṣār's acceptance of the Banu Naḍīr distribution. Qāshānī ascribes it to purity and certainty of their own share. Anas reports a man promised Paradise for bearing no ill will or envy despite modest night worship; the Prophet warned Anṣār of later favoritism and urged patience until the Pool."}, {"id": "59:9/q08/p2", "position": "No desire or claim for the migrants' allotment arises in them.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī takes ḥājah as a needed object; al-Ālūsī prefers this over resentment and says 'find' conveys practical awareness in the chest. Biqāʿī says no inner request, much less an open request. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains 'find' as mental perception and cites a poet's negated perception; ḥājah can mean desired aim as in 40:80 and 12:68, and min marks origin or cause. Qāshānī and the Study Quran extend detachment to worldly shares. Al-Naḥḥās coordinates the clause with 'they love'; Study Quran cites renouncing the world for God's love and renouncing others' goods for people's love."}, {"id": "59:9/q08/p3", "position": "They felt no painful lack from what the migrants received.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr retains literal need as an emotion and says love erased any sense of deprivation; Qurṭubī and Nasafī supply omitted nouns yielding distress at what they missed. Qurṭubī also offers contentment even if the Anṣār's own allotment was small."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q09", "question": "To whom do the pronouns in 'their breasts' and 'they were given' refer?", "turns_on": "Whether both pronouns refer to the Anṣār or the second to emigrants.", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q09/p1", "position": "The breasts belong to Anṣār; those given things are emigrants.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya supplies Banu Naḍīr's villages and property as what the emigrants received. Ibn ʿĀshūr says contextual pronouns can change antecedent nearby, citing 30:9 and poetry; Ṭabāṭabāʾī notes the first plural tracks the Anṣār and second tracks the plural sense of 'who'."}, {"id": "59:9/q09/p2", "position": "Both pronouns refer to the Anṣār, with an omitted possessive before 'need'.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ supplies the omitted muḍāf; Qurṭubī and Nasafī similarly understand their distress over what they themselves lacked."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q10", "question": "What does 'breasts' imply for inward speech and feeling?", "turns_on": "Whether inward wording and meaning count as speech literally or only figuratively in a tangential discussion cited among the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q10/p1", "position": "Inward speech is a mental wording joined to meaning, and 'speech' can apply to it literally.", "reasons": "Ālūsī argues a mentally imagined sentence is a fifth element beyond spoken words and abstract meaning; recalled words can affect a person without sound. He challenges al-Ṭūfī's appeal to frequent verbal usage and defends al-Akhṭal's line, whether it reads bayān or kalām, as evidence of the heart's inward ordering of words."}, {"id": "59:9/q10/p2", "position": "Speech is literal utterance; an inner meaning or the poem's 'speech' is figurative.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭūfī argues listeners immediately understand utterance and that only uttered expression actually affects them; he reads al-Akhṭal's line as bayān or treats kalām there as hyperbole. Ālūsī rejects those arguments."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q11", "question": "What was given, and to how many needy Anṣār?", "turns_on": "Whether the gift is material fayʾ or status, and whether two or three Anṣār were exceptional recipients.", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q11/p1", "position": "Primarily Banu Naḍīr's fayʾ and other wealth or gifts to emigrants.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and others describe the Prophet's distribution. Biqāʿī says the passive can include any giver, even God and His Messenger, and gifts beyond fayʾ; Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies Banu Naḍīr."}, {"id": "59:9/q11/p2", "position": "Three needy Anṣār received fayʾ, named Abū Dujāna, Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, and al-Ḥārith ibn al-Ṣimma.", "reasons": "Bursevī supplies all three names; other sources give the coun

Ṭabarṣī notes divergent counts."}, {"id": "59:9/q11/p4", "position": "The emigrants' rank, honor, closeness, and precedence.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports this alternative; Ibn Kathīr holds that the Anṣār did not envy their favored rank and precedence in mention."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q12", "question": "What does it mean to prefer others over oneself here?", "turns_on": "Whether the omitted recipients are specifically emigrants or people generally, and what the preference comprises.", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q12/p1", "position": "The Anṣār prefer emigrants by sharing homes, wealth, food, and the fayʾ, even while needy.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī and Qurṭubī identify the omitted object as emigrants; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the previous reference makes it recoverable and that this exceeds merely not coveting their gifts. Mujāhid says they received no booty themselves. Bayḍāwī and Nasafī report even an offer involving a wife. Ibn Kathīr compares 76:8 and 2:177 and quotes charity by one with little. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says this praise and the īthār clause describe the Anṣār."}, {"id": "59:9/q12/p2", "position": "They put any other believers or people before themselves.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī leaves recipients general; Ālūsī says the omitted object need not restrict the virtue to emigrants. Elmalılı includes fellow believers more broadly; Asad extends it to refugees. Al-Wāḥidī says īthār is singling out and favoring; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a virtuous choice."}, {"id": "59:9/q12/p3", "position": "Inwardly, altruism prefers God's pleasure or all companions' rights over one's own interest.", "reasons": "Tustarī says preference for God's pleasure proves love; Wahīb's divine oath promises freedom from worries and inner poverty for such preference. Sulamī's authorities define chivalry, companion-first conduct, refusing distinctions, afterlife preference, and seeing one's hand as a trustee of God's property. Qushayrī says true altruism may favor even the full while one hungers and sees one's own goods as a trust. Qāshānī makes it detachment from ego and love of path companions."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q13", "question": "What does īthār mean as a virtue, and when is it appropriate?", "turns_on": "Whether giving all at personal cost is always superior or depends on one's ability to endure hardship.", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q13/p1", "position": "It is choosing another's benefit over one's own, a high form of generosity even in need.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī defines it as favoring and singling out; Qurṭubī traces it to certainty, love and patience, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls costly preference the noblest trait. Ibn Kathīr cites the best charity as the effort of one with little; Study Quran links 2:177 and 76:8. Giving one's life is an even higher form: Qurṭubī and Bursevī cite Abū Ṭalḥa shielding the Prophet at Uḥud and the sacrifice at Yarmūk. Elmalılı says occasion stories exemplify many such acts, including giving up a wife for an emigrant."}, {"id": "59:9/q13/p2", "position": "An inward virtue of placing God and others ahead of ego without distinctions.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥafṣ includes worldly and religious interests; Sulamī's other authorities place every person's rights first and see owned goods as trust. Qushayrī says one may even prefer someone already full and that distinguishing people weakens altruism. Qāshānī calls it restraint from ego's share after tasting universal desires."}, {"id": "59:9/q13/p3", "position": "Giving everything is excellent for one able to bear want; another should retain enough to avoid begging.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reconciles praise of the Anṣār with the Prophet's rebuke of a man who gave away his entire gold piece then would beg, and cites 2:177."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q14", "question": "What historical arrangement with the Anṣār and emigrants is linked to the fayʾ?", "turns_on": "Which choice the Prophet offered and what the Anṣār chose; sources give differing terms.", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q14/p1", "position": "The Prophet offered the Anṣār a fayʾ share if they shared homes and wealth, or their property if they took no fayʾ; they shared their property and left the fayʾ to emigrants.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, Ibn ʿAbbās reports, and others describe the choice at Banu Naḍīr and the Anṣār's selflessness. Wāḥidī and Rāzī prefer this as the sound occasion. One Māwardī version also mentions Qurayẓa's spoils."}, {"id": "59:9/q14/p2", "position": "The Anṣār offered land division; the Prophet kept their land with them and arranged migrant work and shared dates or harvest.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd's Ṭabarī and Māwardī reports give the harvest-and-service alternative; Yazīd ibn al-Aṣamm says the verse followed acceptance. Other reports say the Anṣār offered palms, while the Prophet declined land transfer and organized shared produce; after conquest, loaned palms were returned. Bursevī says the Prophet kept land for cultivation and loaned palms were returned; Ibn Kathīr judges one Anas chain sound by the two Ṣaḥīḥs' standards but notes another chain inserts an unnamed man."}, {"id": "59:9/q14/p3", "position": "The Prophet retained authority over surrendered Banu Naḍīr property and distributed it as he wished.", "reasons": "ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr says it was surrendered to the Prophet; Jishumī relates Muslims asking for it and the property being left to his discretion. Ibn Kathīr connects the Ansar's discussion to the rule of 59:6 that no cavalry won it."}, {"id": "59:9/q14/p4", "position": "The Prophet offered a joint allotment if migrants stayed with Anṣār, or a migrant allotment if they left; the Anṣār chose the migrants' allotment while retaining them as guests.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī names Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda and Saʿd ibn Muʿādh as spokesmen and reports the Prophet's prayer for their families; Biqāʿī gives a version where they also offered property. Fayʾ property was allocated to migrants and needy Anṣār."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q15", "question": "What event occasioned the verse's praise of selflessness?", "turns_on": "Whether the occasion was fayʾ allocation, guest hospitality, a circulated sheep's head, or another sacrifice.", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q15/p1", "position": "An Anṣārī household fed the Prophet's hungry guest its only meal while the family went hungry.", "reasons": "Abū Hurayra's widely transmitted account says the children slept, the lamp was put out, and the couple feigned eating; the Prophet said God marveled or laughed. Sources variously identify the host as Abū Ṭalḥa, Thābit ibn Qays, Abū al-Mutawakkil, or ʿAlī and Fāṭima; some identify the guest as Ahl al-Ṣuffa. Wāḥidī cites Bukhārī and Muslim; Qurtubī grades this the more authentic occasion, while Ibn Kathīr discusses sound chains. Kashf al-Asrār takes the phrase as an allusion to Anṣār hospitality."}, {"id": "59:9/q15/p2", "position": "The Anṣār's preference for emigrants in the Banu Naḍīr fayʾ.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī and Rāzī call this the sound or actual occasion while allowing guest stories as examples within the verse. Qurtubī prefers the guest report. Elmalılı says occasions exemplify a widespread virtue."}, {"id": "59:9/q15/p3", "position": "A sheep's head passed through seven needy households before returning to the first.", "reasons": "Reports from Ibn ʿUmar and other transmitters give seven, with variants as to whether the first recipient was a Companion or Anṣārī; Ḥākim authenticates a version."}, {"id": "59:9/q15/p4", "position": "Wounded men at Yarmūk passed water onward and died without drinking.", "reasons": "Ḥudhayfa al-ʿAdawī's version names his cousin and Hishām ibn al-ʿĀṣ before an unnamed third; Ibn Kathīr gives ʿIkrima and companions; Elmalılı mentions Akif's poetic depiction."}, {"id": "59:9/q15/p5", "position": "Other later acts show the same selflessness without being its initial occasion.", "reasons": "Al-Anṭākī's thirty men left all scarce bread untouched in darkness; ʿĀʾisha gave her only loaf and later received a baked sheep; Ibn ʿUmar repeatedly gave the same returned grape cluster; Abū ʿUbayda and Muʿādh redistributed ʿUmar's 400 dinars. Abū Bakr gave all his wealth. Al-Thaʿlabī and Qurṭubī cite ascetic teachings from a Balkh youth and Dhū al-Nūn."}, {"id": "59:9/q15/p6", "position": "A roasted sheep's head passed among nine needy Companions and returned to its first recipient.", "reasons": "Anas is named in al-Thaʿlabī, Ibn al-Jawzī and Nasafī; they specify nine rather than seven."}, {"id": "59:9/q15/p7", "position": "Seven thirsty men at Uḥud passed a single cup and died without drinking.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Ṭabarṣī place this account at Uḥud and give seven men."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q16", "question": "What does khaṣāṣah mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q16/p1", "position": "Need, poverty, or hunger, with an original image of gaps or openings.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī calls it a verbal noun and noun for need or a gap, with plurals khaṣāṣāt and khaṣāṣ; an anonymous rajaz line pictures eyes looking through wall openings. Others cite holes in walls, doors, sieves, clouds and veils, or a sickly person's poverty relieved by spring; Bursevī cites al-Rāghib on a gapped reed hut. Tustarī notes makhṣūṣ for an impoverished person; Qurtubī and Jishumī also derive it from being left without what one needs."}]}

{"id": "59:9/q18", "question": "How is yūqa read and parsed?", "turns_on": "The common light-qāf reading differs from geminated readings; grammarians also dispute retaining a weak final letter under jussive.", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q18/p1", "position": "The common reading is yūqa with a light qāf, passive imperfect in a jussive condition.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās, Jishumī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya analyze the verb as conditional with the final weak letter deleted; Jishumī makes shuḥḥ its accusative object. Basrans bar retention of the weak alif; Kufans cite poetic 'alam yaʾtīka' and 20:77, but Naḥḥās says they confuse vowels and poetic license."}, {"id": "59:9/q18/p2", "position": "Abū Ḥaywa and Ibn Abī ʿAblah read a doubled qāf, with the wāw opened.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī also names Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ and Abū Rajāʾ for yuwaqqa. The exact transmitters vary among the sources."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q19", "question": "How is shuḥḥ read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q19/p1", "position": "The first consonant has ḍamma in the common reading.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Samīn set this against a kasra variant; Ālūsī says the two have the same meaning."}, {"id": "59:9/q19/p2", "position": "Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn Abī ʿAblah, and Abū Ḥaywa read it with kasra.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya names Ibn ʿUmar; Abū Ḥayyān names Abū Ḥaywa and Ibn Abī ʿAblah; al-Samīn and Ālūsī give Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Abī ʿAblah."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q20", "question": "What is the soul's shuḥḥ, and how does it differ from bukhl?", "turns_on": "Whether shuḥḥ is ordinary stinginess, stronger inner greed, wrongful taking of others' property, or a wider disobedient impulse.", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q20/p1", "position": "It is intense, innate greed or tightness about giving, whose act is bukhl.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and Naḥḥās gloss withholding surplus and cite ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm's miser; al-Khaṭṭābī calls shuḥḥ a general inborn disposition and bukhl an act concerning particulars. Rāzī says the soul bears the impulse and withholding is its effect; Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers 'inner poverty' that wealth worsens. Al-Rāghib says habitual greed plus stinginess; Ālūsī rejects narrow lexicographic definitions but accepts extreme greed that resents others' generosity. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 4:128 and says blame depends on what is withheld. Al-Wāḥidī says greed leads to withholding others' due rights and envy."}, {"id": "59:9/q20/p2", "position": "Specifically, it is wrongfully taking or coveting another person's property; withholding one's own is bukhl.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd repeatedly answers a worried miser that Qur'anic shuḥḥ is consuming a brother's wealth unjustly; Ṭāwūs and Ibn ʿUmar focus on ownership, even lawful coveting. Al-Ḥasan extends covetous looking to another's wife. Ālūsī questions these as formal dictionary definitions while preserving them as instances."}, {"id": "59:9/q20/p3", "position": "It includes withholding obligatory dues and taking the unlawful.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn Jubayr combines forbidden acquisition with withholding zakat; ʿAṭāʾ singles out withholding expenditure; Jishumī says the legal sense is withholding an obligation. Qurṭubī includes zakat, kinship, and hospitality."}, {"id": "59:9/q20/p4", "position": "It is the soul's desire to disobey, injustice, or abandonment of duties.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās identifies desire resisting faith; al-Ḥasan calls it sin; Ibn ʿUyayna calls it injustice; al-Layth calls it leaving obligations and violating prohibitions. Sulamī's Muḥammad ibn al-Faḍl says every miser wrongs another. Islāḥī renders it selfishness and warns of the hypocrites' fate."}, {"id": "59:9/q20/p5", "position": "Inwardly, it is attachment to anything besides God, rooted in the lower soul.", "reasons": "Tustarī and Sahl identify the soul's greed as clinging to anything beyond God and remembrance; Qāshānī calls particular gains native to the lower soul, overcome only through divine protection; al-Wāsiṭī says even exemplary virtues fail if the inner self keeps private interests."}, {"id": "59:9/q20/p6", "position": "Shuḥḥ and bukhl are equivalent names for miserliness.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports this view; Qurṭubī initially treats them as equivalents but later endorses Ibn Masʿūd's distinction."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q21", "question": "What warnings and reports explain the danger of greed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q21/p1", "position": "It destroys faith and communities and drives bloodshed, unlawful acts, and severed kinship.", "reasons": "Prophetic reports transmitted by Jābir, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr and others say avarice destroyed earlier peoples; another says faith and shuḥḥ cannot coexist, paralleling dust from God's path and Hell's smoke. Sources also report that nothing damaged Islam more, that obedient greed is ruinous, and that greed is worse than poverty. Ibn ʿAwf prayed for protection lest he steal or commit adultery."}, {"id": "59:9/q21/p2", "position": "The Garden of Eden excludes the miser when this verse is recited.", "reasons": "Prophetic reports recorded by al-Suyūṭī, Ālūsī and Elmalılı connect Eden's response with 'the believers have succeeded' (23:1), followed by exclusion of a miser."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q22", "question": "How is a person protected from the soul's greed?", "turns_on": "Whether protection is exemplified by specific gifts, fulfilling commands and avoiding prohibitions, or inward release from attachment.", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q22/p1", "position": "By God's aid one resists greed, takes no forbidden thing, and gives what God commands.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd's repeated formulation combines avoiding forbidden taking with fulfilling commanded spending; Ibn Jubayr adds zakat. Muqātil says God shields the Anṣār as they willingly forego fayʾ. Biqāʿī sees the passive as stressing difficulty and divine aid; Ibn ʿĀshūr grades success according to the degree of protection."}, {"id": "59:9/q22/p2", "position": "Paying zakat, hosting guests, and helping in hardship suffice to free a person of it.", "reasons": "Prophetic reports recur across Ṭabarī, Thaʿlabī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurṭubī and later sources. ʿAlī says zakat alone protects. Ālūsī and Elmalılı say total generosity in every matter is unnecessary. Ibn ʿUmar's disputed example of money he wished back and approving ʿUthmān's death shows how widely the charge could be applied."}, {"id": "59:9/q22/p3", "position": "Protection frees the heart from any claim beyond God and from ego's self-interest.", "reasons": "Tustarī and Sahl say the protected abide with God; al-Wāsiṭī warns that even the virtues of Moses, Abraham, and the Beloved cannot compensate for an innermost self that still sees its own stake. Al-Qushayrī distinguishes being protected from merely abstaining; al-Suhrawardī contrasts innate liberality with acquired giving."}, {"id": "59:9/q22/p4", "position": "The Anṣār exhibited protection by voluntarily leaving fayʾ to emigrants.", "reasons": "Maqātil, Wāḥidī and Ibn al-Jawzī give this concrete application; Anas swore there were no misers among the Anṣār, and Bursevī quotes a report making the same claim."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q23", "question": "Why is protection from greed worded and placed as a conditional conclusion?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q23/p1", "position": "It sums up the Anṣār's example as a general rule and emphatically praises those whom God protects.", "reasons": "Qushayrī stresses 'is protected' rather than simple avoidance; Biqāʿī says the passive evokes strong divine aid. Bursevī calls the close an aside about Anṣār; Ibn ʿĀshūr an epilogue explaining their altruism. Ālūsī says singular man followed by plural ulāʾika tracks form then sense, suggesting few attain this great rank."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q24", "question": "Who are the successful, and what is their success?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q24/p1", "position": "Those protected from greed attain their sought good and escape harm, especially Paradise and reward.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says they remain in Paradise; Ibn ʿAṭiyya glosses mufliḥūn as attaining what they seek; Bayḍāwī names present praise and future reward; Bursevī calls it happiness in both abodes. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the demonstrative honors them and emphatic restriction magnifies their success, with partial protection bringing proportional success."}, {"id": "59:9/q24/p2", "position": "Inwardly, success is attaining the heart's perfections and life with God.", "reasons": "Qāshānī identifies the heart's perfections; Sahl and Tustarī say freedom from attachment yields abiding with God."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q25", "question": "What legal consequence follows from resentment of the Companions?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q25/p1", "position": "One who disparages or resents a Companion has no entitlement to Muslim fayʾ.", "reasons": "Mālik cites the sequence of fayʾ distribution and the prayer for later believers in 59:7–10."}]}

{"id": "59:9/q27", "question": "How does the verse fit the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "Whether it continues a distribution list or forms a parenthetic praise and ethical contrast.", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q27/p1", "position": "It continues the fayʾ recipients and praises Anṣār after the emigrants.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says allocation first honors emigrants, then consoles and thanks Anṣār; Ibn ʿĀshūr joins them for coherence and treats the closing condition as a general epilogue. Kur'an Yolu reads 59:8–10 as an ideal of selfless believers and respect across generations."}, {"id": "59:9/q27/p2", "position": "It is a fresh praise of Anṣār after an emigrant-only allotment.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī bases this on distinct Banu Naḍīr allocations; Ibn ʿĀshūr reports and rejects such a break as damaging coherence."}, {"id": "59:9/q27/p3", "position": "Verses 5–10 are a parenthesis answering Jewish and hypocrite objections to Banu Naḍīr events.", "reasons": "Islāḥī treats this as a digression from the main story and says Anṣār's contentment shames hypocrites who demanded booty; he warns that the hypocrites' selfishness threatens their fate."}]}
{"id": "59:9/q28", "question": "What conduct does the verse commend for later believers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "59:9/q28/p1", "position": "Love of the Anṣār is a mark of faith; honor them and pardon their faults.", "reasons": "ʿUmar counsels the next caliph to safeguard early emigrants' rights and accept Anṣār good while forgiving faults. Bursevī quotes the Prophet that loving Anṣār signals faith and hating them hypocrisy, plus a prayer for them and their descendants."}, {"id": "59:9/q28/p2", "position": "Welcome and share with needy believers, seek God's pleasure, keep faith sincere, and ask divine help against selfishness.", "reasons": "Islāḥī says the historical sacrifice teaches mutual sympathy and generosity. Asad applies the Anṣār's welcome to refugees in every age."}, {"id": "59:9/q28/p3", "position": "Religion is love and the Anṣār's love illustrates it.", "reasons": "Imam al-Bāqir links this verse with 3:31 and 49:7 and concludes that religion and love are one."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q01", "question": "How does the opening pronoun and name function?", "turns_on": "Whether huwa is a pronoun of matter or resumes the preceding divine name.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q01/p1", "position": "He is a pronoun of matter, with the following sentence as its predicate.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur refers to the preceding verse for the same analysis."}, {"id": "59:24/q01/p2", "position": "He refers back to God's preceding name; Allah is its predicate and al-Khāliq its attribute.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur gives this as the alternative parse."}, {"id": "59:24/q01/p3", "position": "The pronoun truly applies to God alone, the necessary being.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī contrasts God's existence through Himself with contingent beings that might not exist."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q02", "question": "What does the name Allah signify here?", "turns_on": "The reported etymologies differ; the theological descriptions address the name's function.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q02/p1", "position": "Allah uniquely names the divine Essence, gathering all perfections; the other names describe it.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī calls it the familiar true name without namesake; Elmalılı treats al-Raḥmān as exclusive too; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says its repetition in three verses reinforces the point."}, {"id": "59:24/q02/p2", "position": "Allah's derivation is from ilāh, its article replacing the hamza.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj transmits al-Khalīl through Sībawayh."}, {"id": "59:24/q02/p3", "position": "Allah's original form is lāh, with an inseparable definite article.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj reports al-Khalīl's other derivation."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q03", "question": "Why identify God as the Creator and repeat Allah?", "turns_on": "Whether sole creation itself establishes exclusive divinity or requires the premise of sovereign lordship.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q03/p1", "position": "God alone truly creates, so alleged partners have no creative power and no claim to worship.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī excludes any co-creator; Ibn ʿĀshūr finds exclusivity in the definite subject and predicate and cites 16:20, 16:17. Al-Biqāʿī says all acts, visible and unseen, are His, opposing the Qadariyya; Elmalılı says human art cannot originate even an atom. Islahi draws the duty of worship."}, {"id": "59:24/q03/p2", "position": "God's unique creation alone does not establish exclusive worship, since idolaters admit His creation yet worship other lords.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes creation names here from the preceding verses' lordship and sovereign management, which entail worship."}, {"id": "59:24/q03/p3", "position": "The Qurʾān does not leave people merely to predestination.", "reasons": "Muṭarrif ibn al-Shikhkhīr is reported with this assertion in Muqātil's discussion of the verse."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q04", "question": "What does al-Khāliq mean?", "turns_on": "Whether khalq stresses prior determination, origination without a model, or a broader process of formation.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q04/p1", "position": "The one who measures, determines, and plans what He brings into existence according to will and wisdom.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās cites poetry for khalq as measuring; al-Thaʿlabī and al-Baghawī cite 39:6 and successive states, and al-Thaʿlabī 71:14. Zuhayr's line, cited by Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī, contrasts executing a plan with empty wishes. Ibn Kathīr's cutter measures before cutting; al-Biqāʿī uses the shoemaker. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites al-Rāghib's sound proportioning and al-Kashshāf's gloss. Al-Ṭabrisī separately reports a wise determination followed by willing origination."}, {"id": "59:24/q04/p2", "position": "The initiator who brings what did not exist into being without prior material or model.", "reasons": "Al-Khaṭṭābī calls Him inventor without a model. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls origination the dominant divine-name sense and cites 50:38, distinguishing it from image-making; al-ʿArabī's broader formulation includes qualities. Al-Ṭabrisī includes bodies and accidents."}, {"id": "59:24/q04/p3", "position": "Creation can mean producing one thing from another or forming a thing in a specific shape.", "reasons": "Elmalılı and al-Ālūsī record the broader material sense. Ibn ʿĀshūr notes Jesus' forming a clay bird at 3:49."}, {"id": "59:24/q04/p4", "position": "In inward interpretation, He measures manifestations according to His names and attributes.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī relates creation to the appearance of divine names."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q05", "question": "What does al-Bāriʾ mean, and what is its scope?", "turns_on": "The proposed roots and usage differ, especially whether the name denotes origination, differentiation, adjustment, or a restricted class of creatures.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q05/p1", "position": "The originator who brings creatures from nonexistence into existence.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī ascribes it to divine power; al-Māwardī cites poetry; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Bursawī add freedom from disproportion, and Ibn Kathīr emphasizes carrying out the determined plan. Al-Naḥḥās reports Ibn ʿUrafa's origination without prior model, addition, or subtraction. Al-Ṭabrisī includes bodies and accidents; Ibn ʿĀshūr reports al-Ghazālī's origination gloss but rejects it as contrary to usage."}, {"id": "59:24/q05/p2", "position": "The one who separates, differentiates, and distinguishes creatures or their forms.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī appeals to separating oneself from someone; al-Kashshāf and Ibn ʿĀshūr use varied shapes, and the latter prefers this over other glosses. Al-Biqāʿī adds refining and repairing what was measured; limited makers leave defects. Ṭabāṭabāʾī and al-Qāshānī also stress differentiation."}, {"id": "59:24/q05/p3", "position": "The one who proportions and adjusts what was previously measured.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās prefers this distinct act; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Bursawī stress freedom from disproportion and defect, and Elmalılı orderly completion."}, {"id": "59:24/q05/p4", "position": "The maker or originator specifically of bodies, not accidents such as color or taste.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī cites the term bariyya for corporeal creatures; Elmalılı reports his distinction. Al-Ṭabrisī instead explicitly includes both bodies and accidents."}, {"id": "59:24/q05/p5", "position": "Creation especially of living beings or animals, without a prior model.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭi prefers Ibn al-Athīr's distinction, citing 2:54 and 98:6–7, while 57:22 shows rare nonliving use. Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects restriction to humans with 98:6–7, a hadith and ʿAlī's saying; al-Rāghib glosses bariyya as creatures."}, {"id": "59:24/q05/p6", "position": "Creation specifically of

humankind from dust.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports Ibn al-ʿArabī's derivation from dust and interpretation of bariyya in 98:6–7 as people, then cites evidence that the term is wider."}, {"id": "59:24/q05/p7", "position": "It is essentially synonymous with al-Khāliq, creator.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās calls this loose usage, perhaps eased by the adjacent al-Khāliq. {"id": "59:24/q06", "question": "What does al-Muṣawwir mean?", "turns_on": "Whether form refers to visible outlines alone, inward qualities too, or the changing stages of living creatures.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q06/p1", "position": "The one who gives creatures their distinct forms and appearances as He wills.", "reasons": "Muqātil details sex, color and bodily soundness in the womb; al-Thaʿlabī and Ibn al-Jawzī stress recognizable differences. Al-Rāghib, cited by al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı, distinguishes sensible and intellectual forms and cites 7:11; al-Ṭabrisī includes animals and inanimate things. Elmalılı cites 3:6 and 82:7; Ibn Kathīr 82:8."}, {"id": "59:24/q06/p2", "position": "The shaper of developing humans through successive womb forms or stages of life.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī cites al-Nābigha's line, from sperm to clot to flesh and age; Muqātil describes limbs emerging from the lump, while al-Qurṭubī gives clot, lump and recognizable form."}, {"id": "59:24/q06/p3", "position": "In inward interpretation, He forms the detailed manifestations of His attributes.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī links outward form to divine attributes."}, {"id": "59:24/q06/p4", "position": "God's form-giving embraces both visible shapes and intellectual or spiritual qualities.", "reasons": "Al-Rāghib's division in al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı; Kuran Yolu stresses sensory and nonsensory, material and spiritual characteristics."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q07", "question": "What is the derivation of al-Muṣawwir?", "turns_on": "The root consonant and required participial form.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q07/p1", "position": "It derives from ṣūra and ṣawwara, meaning image or form.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and Makkī reject a derivation from ṣāra/yaṣīru because that would require yāʾ or yield al-muṣīr, and it misses the meaning."}, {"id": "59:24/q07/p2", "position": "It derives from ṣāra/yaṣīru.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās transmits this alternative only to reject it on morphology; Makkī also rejects it."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q08", "question": "How do the three creation names relate and why this order?", "turns_on": "Whether the three names denote causal phases, biological development, inseparable perspectives, or progressively narrower acts.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q08/p1", "position": "They mark determination, bringing into existence, and final shaping, in that sequence.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī argues will's choice precedes power's effect and essences precede attributes. Ibn Kathīr uses a measured cut, al-Biqāʿī a building plan and prepared materials, and al-Ghazālī an ordered act. Al-Qurṭubī rejects equating creation with image-making; al-Nābigha's verse supports the order. Al-Ṭabarī's terms and subsequent sources follow it."}, {"id": "59:24/q08/p2", "position": "They describe the successive development of creatures, especially the human embryo in the womb.", "reasons": "Muqātil names seed, clot, lump, limbs and chosen traits; al-Thaʿlabī gives staged completion; al-Qurṭubī and al-Nābigha describe womb stages. Study Quran transmits this as an alternative."}, {"id": "59:24/q08/p3", "position": "The names distinguish inseparable perspectives on the same act of creating.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports al-Ghazālī's account but says it does not fit the names' usage."}, {"id": "59:24/q08/p4", "position": "The names narrow from originating things, to making bodies, to visible shaping.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports Ibn al-ʿArabī's hierarchy and says it blends two senses; his own staged account invokes 82:7–8 and 3:6."}, {"id": "59:24/q08/p5", "position": "Al-Bāriʾ and al-Muṣawwir form one semantic unit.", "reasons": "Asad cites al-Bayḍāwī for reading Maker and Shaper together."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q09", "question": "How is al-Muṣawwir read and parsed?", "turns_on": "The vowels and case ending determine whether the word names God, the fashioned object, or a construct phrase.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q09/p1", "position": "The common reading has kasra on wāw and nominative rāʾ: an adjective or predicate of God.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn records the two parses. Al-Zajjāj rejects a transmitted accusative al-bāriʾa al-muṣawwira."}, {"id": "59:24/q09/p2", "position": "With fatḥa on wāw and accusative rāʾ, it is the formed object governed by al-Bāriʾ.", "reasons": "Reports attribute it variously to ʿAlī, Ḥāṭib, al-Ḥasan, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ/Ibn al-Sumayqiʿ; the object is Adam, descendants, forms generally, or in al-Kashshāf's wording a form-giver. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it good; al-Samīn and al-Burhān say al-Bāriʾ governs it and one must not pause after al-Bāriʾ. Al-Zajjāj rejects a related accusative."}, {"id": "59:24/q09/p3", "position": "With fatḥa on wāw and genitive rāʾ, an active participle is annexed to its object.", "reasons": "Reported from ʿAlī; Ibn ʿAṭiyya compares al-ḥasan al-wajh, al-Samīn says annexation lightens the phrase and disallows pausing at the word."}, {"id": "59:24/q09/p4", "position": "An accusative with kasra on wāw can be parsed as a detached accusative of praise.", "reasons": "Makkī rejects its construction as object of the prior participle; al-Samīn parses a confirmed report by detachment and compares 1:1."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q10", "question": "Does a reading of al-Muṣawwir with an open wāw affect prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q10/p1", "position": "Al-Khāniyya says that it invalidates prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports the ruling, allowing it if the word is wrongly construed as God's attribute but questioning it otherwise."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q11", "question": "How is al-Bāriʾ pronounced in one transmitted reading?", "turns_on": "Which transmission from al-Dūrī and al-Kisāʾī is followed.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q11/p1", "position": "Most Maghribī authorities report imāla for al-Dūrī from al-Kisāʾī.", "reasons": "Ibn Farḥ's route also transmits imāla, treating it like bāriʾukum."}, {"id": "59:24/q11/p2", "position": "Abū ʿUthmān al-Ḍarīr and most reading sources report fatḥ.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī contrasts their transmission with the Maghribī imāla reports."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q12", "question": "Why are the creation names listed without conjunctions?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q12/p1", "position": "They are successive descriptors of one referent, functioning as praise without conjunction.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān calls this taʿdīd; al-Itqān says the sequence praises and glorifies; al-Biqāʿī says each name reveals what the prior implies and their totality conveys Allah."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q13", "question": "What do 'the most beautiful names' denote, and why are they beautiful?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase is explained through the names' qualities, their scope, or their relation to the single divine Essence.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q13/p1", "position": "God's names denote supremely beautiful and perfect attributes and meanings.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī derives their beauty from attributes; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says these meanings subsist in God's essence. He lists examples from the Qurʾān and Prophetic invocation, including exclusive names."}, {"id": "59:24/q14/p2", "position": "The listed names sum up power and knowledge as the roots of perfection.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī says all perfections return to them; al-Biqāʿī notes wisdom in fashioning and the limits of human comprehension."}, {"id": "59:24/q14/p3", "position": "The passage provides seventeen divine names, or eighteen if huwa is counted.", "reasons": "Study Quran calls it the Qurʾān's most extensive list."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q15", "question": "What divine names are proclaimed in the reported gathering on Judgment Day?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q15/p1", "position": "God gathers the seven heavens and earth in His grasp and declares a series of His names.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUmar transmits a Prophetic report of God's words; the excerpt breaks off during the list."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q16", "question": "May God be named with fitting terms not found in scripture?", "turns_on": "Whether divine naming requires transmitted wording or a meaning befitting God's majesty.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q16/p1", "position": "Only terms established in the Qurʾān or authentic hadith may be used as divine names.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī reports the restrictive view, citing ʿĀlim, ʿAlīm, ʿAllām and excluding unattested ʿĀrif, Faqīh, Mutayaqqin."}, {"id": "59:24/q16/p2", "position": "Any fitting term conveying divine perfection may be used.", "reasons": "The permissive side invokes accepted Persian, Turkish and Indian descriptions and 17:110's stress on beautiful meanings. Al-Bursawī says new terms with unsound implications are discourteous, but sound and beautiful ones are permissible."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q17", "question": "What etiquette governs using and invoking particular names?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q17/p1", "position": "Names of acts should be used with scriptural decorum and some opposing attributes paired.", "reasons": "Elmalılı cautions against calling God simply creator of apes and pigs, and rejects Muʿtazilī denial that He creates evil while preferring 'creator of good and evil.' Al-Bayhaqī pairs al-Ḍārr with al-Nāfiʿ (22:13); Elmalılı similarly pairs al-Qābiḍ with al-Bāsiṭ (2:245) and notes might with retribution."}, {"id": "59:24/q17/p2", "position": "The names can be invoked with attention to their grammatical article and root.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī reports that knowers attend to both, while the Malāmiyya omit the article as additional to the root; scholars distinguish name, named, and naming."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q18", "question": "How many names does God have, and what does enumerating ninety-nine mean?", "turns_on": "Whether ninety-nine is exhaustive, and whether enumeration means counting, knowing, or observing the names.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q18/p1", "position": "A Prophetic report promises Paradise to whoever enumerates God's ninety-nine names, one fewer than one hundred.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Zajjāj, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and others transmit it, often through Abū Hurayra; Ibn Kathīr and Elmalılı cite the Ṣaḥīḥayn and add that God is One and loves odd numbers. Al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Mājah and al-Bayhaqī transmit lists with variant wording; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says no particular list is firmly established."}, {"id": "59:24/q18/p2", "position": "The ninety-nine are not an exhaustive limit; God has other, even unrevealed names.", "reasons": "The Prophet's supplication asks by names revealed, taught or reserved in unseen knowledge. Elmalılı cites Ibn Masʿūd and ʿĀʾisha's prayers and names in Qurʾān and Sunna beyond enumerated lists; al-Rāzī reports a dhikr book with four thousand. Elmalılı even infers al-Witr as a further name from the odd-number hadith."}, {"id": "59:24/q18/p3", "position": "Enumerating can mean learning and counting the knowable names or carefully observing their bounds in one's dealings with God.", "reasons": "Elmalılı links it to knowing God, answered prayer and the significance of odd numbers; the three after-prayer remembrances of 33 each total 99."}, {"id": "59:24/q18/p4", "position": "God has four thousand names in a reported dhikr book.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī quotes al-Rāzī: one thousand in Qurʾān and sound reports and one thousand each in Torah, Gospel and Psalms."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q19", "question": "Where is God's greatest name identified in this passage?", "turns_on": "The transmitted locations and identification of the greatest name differ.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q19/p1", "position": "It occurs in the final six verses of Sūrat al-Ḥashr.", "reasons": "Reported from the Prophet through Ibn ʿAbbās; al-Durr and Elmalılı also transmit this location."}, {"id": "59:24/q19/p2", "position": "It is sought in the ending of Sūrat al-Ḥashr, to be recited often.", "reasons": "Abū Hurayra reports asking the Prophet and receiving this repeated direction; al-Kashshāf, al-Qurṭubī and al-Nasafī transmit it."}, {"id": "59:24/q19/p3", "position": "The name Allah itself is the greatest name.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj reports this exegetical identification; Jābir ibn Zayd points to the present verse."}, {"id": "59:24/q19/p4", "position": "The first ten verses of al-Ḥadīd together with al-Ḥashr's ending precede an invocation by the greatest name.", "reasons": "ʿAlī instructs al-Barāʾ in a prayer said to be taught by the Prophet through Gabriel; al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı transmit the report."}, {"id": "59:24/q19/p5", "position": "Invocation by all known and unknown names, including the supreme name, is taught in a report from ʿĀʾisha.", "reasons": "After ablution and two cycles of prayer, the Prophet affirms her supplication."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q20", "question": "What is said about invoking or embodying the creation names?", "turns_on": "The practices differ in the name, number, and promised effect.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q20/p1", "position": "A servant of al-Khāliq plans in accord with God's determination.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī says the divine attribute of measure is disclosed to him."}, {"id": "59:24/q20/p2", "position": "A servant of al-Bāriʾ works in balance and consistency.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī relates this to the absence of disparity in creation."}, {"id": "59:24/q20/p3", "position": "Specified recitations of al-Khāliq are said to bring illumination or recovery of what is lost.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī recommends an hour or more at midnight for heart and face; al-Suhrawardī prescribes 5,000 repetitions of an Idrīsī invocation for a lost thing or distant person."}, {"id": "59:24/q20/p4", "position": "Specified invocations of al-Bāriʾ are said to bring protection, wealth, honor, or healing.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī prescribes 100 repetitions daily for seven days; al-Suhrawardī describes an Idrīsī invocation and an inscription on pitch for illness or madness."}, {"id": "59:24/q20/p5", "position": "A name's abjad count is used as an exact recitation number in retreat.", "reasons": "Al-Bisṭāmī omits the article and calls for a quiet retreat; al-Bursawī compares exact number to a key's teeth, with excess wasteful and shortfall deficient."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q21", "question": "Who or what glorifies God?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause is taken distributively of all created things or specifically of rational beings.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q21/p1", "position": "Everything in heaven and earth, including the heavens and earth themselves, glorifies Him.", "reasons": "Muqātil explains all as remembering and affirming oneness; al-Ṭabarī adds prostration willingly or unwillingly. Ibn Kathīr and Elmalılı cite 17:44. Ṭabāṭabāʾī explicitly includes heaven and earth."}, {"id": "59:24/q21/p2", "position": "Rational beings in heaven and earth glorify God on recognizing His attributes.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr describes each kind's response as intentional or otherwise; even an atheist admiring order unknowingly praises the free agent."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q22", "question": "How do creatures glorify God?", "turns_on": "Whether tasbīḥ is actual speech, disclosure through created form and order, or both.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q22/p1", "position": "Living beings speak praise, while inanimate things show God's transcendence through their state and form.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī divides living and nonliving; al-Naḥḥās says creation reveals a maker without equal. Al-Ālūsī mentions wisdom and benefit as its language of state; Ibn ʿĀshūr treats order, provision and subjugation as signs and says even naturalists indirectly praise."}, {"id": "59:24/q22/p2", "position": "Every created thing has actual glorifying speech in its own manner, though people cannot understand all of it.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports many mystics' view; Ibn Kathīr cites 17:44, and al-Ṭabarī says all prostrate willingly or unwillingly."}, {"id": "59:24/q22/p3", "position": "Glorification is the verbal declaration that God is free of evil and deficiency.", "reasons": "Al-Musayyib and Muqātil gloss subḥān Allāh; ʿAlī says God approved the formula for Himself. Muqātil notes other Qurʾānic contexts where tasbīḥ conveys wonder (17:1, 36:36) or prayer (30:17)."}]}
